findings.reason: a node implementing this literally either duplicates the walk it means to avoid or needs an extra hook (a rebuild callback, or a stamp set recomputed by walking at arm time) that the plan should name; without it the detector's correctness on the second and later passes is unstated.
findings.text: the fast signal's cached stamps are refreshed "again after each rebuild of that tree's index", but nothing in the plan says how the watch learns a rebuild happened: the rebuild is lazy and triggered by a later `/_index` reader, and `_load_dir_stamps` reads the persisted file, which is rewritten only *by* that rebuild — so reading it right after the detector fires the invalidation still returns the pre-change stamps. Left as written, the first detected change leaves the cached stamp permanently unequal to the current `_dir_identity`, and the fast pass re-fires `_invalidate_tree_views` every 10 s for that tree, so the metadata index never settles and `/_index` re-walks the tree on every request — the cost the section exists to avoid

findings.reason: the mechanism is unchanged and correct, and line 43 already states the always-on cost, so only this cost-rationale sentence needs correcting; it does not redirect the node's implementation.
findings.text: "The detector costs stat calls only, only while a tree has readers" is not true of the fast signal as line 43 describes it: the fast pass runs "every 10 s by default" over every mounted tree with no reader condition (line 43's own "36 reads every 10 s across 18 mounted trees"), and only the slow signal is reader-gated (line 44, "A tree nobody is reading pays nothing"). The clause generalises the slow signal's rule to both signals
